analysis.one_liner: Strips courts' deference to the consumer bureau's interpretation of financial laws.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by one House member with no cosponsors, died in committee without a hearing or vote as the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the law governing the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau so that courts give no special weight to the bureau's own reading of the consumer financial laws it enforces. Instead, judges would decide all legal questions about bureau rules and enforcement actions fresh, with no deference. That would make bureau rules and enforcement cases easier to challenge and overturn in court.
analysis.who_benefits: Financial companies facing CFPB rules or enforcement actions. Under current law, courts treat the bureau as the lead expert on the meaning of consumer financial laws; the bill would replace that with fresh judicial review, giving regulated companies more ways to delay, weaken, or overturn the rules they are subject to.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the statutory provision that says courts apply the same deference to the CFPB's interpretation of a consumer financial law as if it were the only agency authorized to apply and enforce that law.

Requires courts reviewing any CFPB action to decide de novo all relevant questions of law, including the meaning of constitutional and statutory provisions and bureau rules, meaning judges start fresh rather than deferring to the agency.
Bars any law from exempting a civil action for judicial review of a CFPB action from this standard unless the law specifically names this subsection, so the rule could not be bypassed indirectly.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers who rely on the bureau to police mortgages, credit cards, debt collection, and other financial products. Weakening the legal weight of the bureau's interpretations makes its rules and enforcement cases harder to sustain, raising the cost of writing and enforcing protections.

drawbacks.text: The bill responds to a real complaint: the CFPB is an executive agency whose interpretations of the very statutes it enforces currently carry special weight in court, and supporters argue fresh judicial review is ordinary constitutional accountability for an unusually powerful regulator.

The cost an honest supporter would acknowledge: if the bureau's rules are easier to overturn, enforcement against financial firms becomes slower and less predictable, and the protections that enforcement produces get weaker for consumers.

The bill also broadens court access beyond its headline, applying the de novo standard in any action for judicial review of a bureau action, which multiplies the opportunities for regulated companies to relitigate bureau decisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's gains go to regulated financial companies, whose compliance and litigation burden falls when agency interpretations carry less legal weight. The cost falls on consumers, who would face a consumer-protection bureau whose rules and enforcement actions are easier to knock down in court. The bill carried no offsetting consumer benefit; it was purely a reduction in the bureau's practical power, and it died without moving.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee: referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, sent to a Financial Services subcommittee a month later, and never marked up, reported, or voted on before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mia Love introduced the bill on June 15, 2016, and it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and the House Judiciary Committee.
No other member cosponsored the bill.
On July 20, 2016, the bill was referred to the Financial Services Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law.
The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, and it expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers and the CFPB's enforcement authority are better off that the bill died, since the bureau's interpretations of consumer financial law kept their full legal weight. Financial firms hoping for easier court challenges to the bureau's rules did not get them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers, and the CFPB's enforcement power

for.name: Rep. Mia Love
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill; it was her only connection to it as no member cosponsored.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever held and the only record of support is a single Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors, so no partisan breakdown exists.

industries.industry: Banks and financial companies regulated by the CFPB
industries.note: If passed, the bill would have made the bureau's rules and enforcement actions easier to challenge and overturn in court by removing judicial deference to the bureau's legal interpretations. The industry's gain comes directly at the cost of the consumer protections the bureau enforces.
